newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK retailer Lane Crawford seen in red in FY 96/97.
newsitem.headline: HK retailer Lane Crawford seen in red in FY 96/97.

text.p: Wheelock and Co Ltd said on Tuesday it expected its retail unit Lane Crawford International Ltd to post a loss in the year to March 31, 1997, but looked forward to better days in the following year.
"We still expect a loss (for the full year). How much I can't tell you," Wheelock managing director John Hung said in an interview.

The upmarket department store operator, in which Wheelock has a 71 percent stake, posted an interim net loss of HK$90.8 million for the six months to September 30, 1996, the first half of its 1996/97 fiscal year.
The interim net included an exceptional loss of HK$33.7 million due mainly to the cost of closing its Singapore store and its Lane Crawford Express operation.
"Things are picking up," Hung said. "Now that we've cut Singapore off we are looking forward to better days.
"But don't forget the loss of Singapore is still carried in the final, so you know I don't see this year to be much better than last year.
"Maybe a year from now, when we've written off all that, in '98, we'll have a better position," he said.
Lane Crawford post a net profit of HK$16.4 million in 1995/96, down 87.5 percent on the previous year.
The retailer closed its money-losing Singapore operation last September.
"Lane Crawford had had hard years since '95. It suffered from the very poor market position in Singapore," Hung said.
The company now operates department stores in Hong Kong and China, where the retail markets also are not buoyant.
But Hung said retail sentiment in Hong Kong was expected to improve marginally this year.
"Hong Kong, you know, it's a tough market still, but it's not the worst...there are signs that it's come off the bottom. But it's still not great," he said.
"Hong Kong, the major stores are okay. It's in the black but not huge margin. We hope that later on in the year we will do better," he said.
The firm has renovated stores and kept down inventories in Hong Kong to cope with the tough situation, he said.
Hung said Lane Crawford's China operation was losing money.
"China is still losing money," he said, declining to divulge figures. "I'm not talking about a very large figure."
"But in China we are not too concerned about losing money because it's what we call an investment phase," he said. "We are quite sure that in time the China market will turn."
